topic.title: Pythagoras and trigonometry in 3D (space diagonals, angle between a line and a plane)
topic.subject: maths
topic.examWeightHint: M8 is two 75-minute papers of 50 marks: Paper 1 non-calculator, Paper 2 calculator. This topic is a Paper 2 fixture, almost always in the last third of the paper, and it is set in three shapes. The common one is a cuboid in two parts worth 5 marks: the space diagonal for 2, then the angle it makes with the base (or with the largest face) for 3 — Summer 2025 P2 Q12, Summer 2023 P2 Q12. The second is the angle alone for 3 marks — Summer 2024 P2 Q11, November 2023 P2 Q12. The third is a 6-mark solid where the required angle sits in a triangle with no right angle, so two Pythagoras steps feed the cosine rule (November 2021 P2 Q11); that last step belongs to the sine and cosine rule topic. Paper 1 sets the same ideas in surd form: a cube's edge from a 9 cm space diagonal for 3 marks (November 2023 P1 Q11) and a space diagonal from surd side lengths for 5 marks (Summer 2022 P1 Q14). Schemes run MA1 for the sum of the squares, A1 for the root, then MA1 for identifying the angle, MA1 for the ratio and A1 for the value.
mustMemorise: Space diagonal of a cuboid: d² = a² + b² + c², which is two Pythagoras steps joined at the base diagonal
Pythagoras and SOHCAHTOA work only in a right-angled triangle, so the first job is always to find one and redraw it in 2-D
The angle between a line and a plane is the angle between the line and its shadow on that plane
Cuboid: the shadow of the space diagonal AG on the base is the base diagonal AC, so the angle is ∠GAC
Cube of edge x: face diagonal x√2, space diagonal x√3
Pyramid: half the base diagonal goes with a slant edge, half the base edge goes with a sloping face; the face is the steeper
Cone: l² = r² + h², with the slant height as the hypotenuse
Keep roots exact until the final line, then round once
notOnThisSpec: 3-D coordinates and 3-D vectors — the Teacher Guidance for M8-GM-03 names only the space diagonal and the angle between a line and a plane, and no paper read sets them
The angle between two planes other than a sloping face and the base (a general dihedral angle)
Non-right triangles inside a solid, where the cosine rule finishes the work (November 2021 M8 Paper 2 Q11) — that step is examined under M8-GM-01 and is taught in the sine and cosine rule topic
Surface area and volume of the solids used here; those belong to the mensuration topics

mustBeAbleTo: Find the right-angled triangle inside a cuboid, pyramid, wedge, prism or cone that contains the length or angle asked for, and draw it again on its own in 2-D with its letters and lengths
Find the space diagonal of a cuboid, either as two Pythagoras steps joined at the base diagonal or in the single line d² = a² + b² + c²
Find the angle between a space diagonal and the base, naming it in three letters before calculating (the shadow of AG on the base is AC, so the angle is ∠GAC)
Find the angle between a space diagonal and a named face, by using that face's diagonal and the edge perpendicular to it
Find the angle between the slant edge of a square-based pyramid and the base, using half the base diagonal
Find the angle between a sloping face of a pyramid and the base, using the perpendicular height and half the base edge
Use the slant height of a cone or pyramid, and tell it apart from the vertical height
Answer show-that parts by finishing on the printed length, and give lengths in surd form on Paper 1
Work backwards: find the edge of a cube from its space diagonal, or a height from a given angle

sheet.howExamined: M8 is two 75-minute papers of 50 marks: Paper 1 non-calculator, Paper 2 calculator. This topic is a Paper 2 fixture, almost always in the last third of the paper, and it is set in three shapes. The common one is a cuboid in two parts worth 5 marks: the space diagonal for 2, then the angle it makes with the base (or with the largest face) for 3 — Summer 2025 P2 Q12, Summer 2023 P2 Q12. The second is the angle alone for 3 marks — Summer 2024 P2 Q11, November 2023 P2 Q12. The third is a 6-mark solid where the required angle sits in a triangle with no right angle, so two Pythagoras steps feed the cosine rule (November 2021 P2 Q11); that last step belongs to the sine and cosine rule topic. Paper 1 sets the same ideas in surd form: a cube's edge from a 9 cm space diagonal for 3 marks (November 2023 P1 Q11) and a space diagonal from surd side lengths for 5 marks (Summer 2022 P1 Q14). Schemes run MA1 for the sum of the squares, A1 for the root, then MA1 for identifying the angle, MA1 for the ratio and A1 for the value.
traps: Finding the diagonal and then stopping, or guessing at the angle: most of the entry found the space diagonal and under half identified the required angle (Summer 2025 M8 Paper 2 Q12)
Measuring the angle from an edge of the base instead of from the base diagonal, which makes ∠GAB out of ∠GAC (Summer 2023 M8 Paper 2 Q12, Summer 2025 M8 Paper 2 Q12)
Using only two of the three dimensions, so a face diagonal is offered as the space diagonal (Summer 2025 M8 Paper 2 Q12)
Working inside the 3-D picture without redrawing the triangle: examiners tied full marks to well laid out solutions with the triangle set out separately (November 2024 M8 Paper 2 Q13)
In a pyramid, using half the base diagonal for a sloping face, or half the base edge for a slant edge; the two angles differ and the face is always the steeper (November 2024 M8 Paper 2 Q13)

Rounding the base diagonal before the trigonometry: √97 rounded to 9.8 moves the angle from 14.2° to 14.3°, and the accuracy mark with it (CCEA General Marking Advice viii, Summer 2025 M4 mark scheme)
Giving the complement, by working from the vertical edge or the vertical height rather than from the base
Treating the slant height of a cone or pyramid as the vertical height, or subtracting when the hypotenuse is the unknown
Mixing metres and centimetres in one Pythagoras line when a context gives both
Stopping at the sum of the squares: 169 is a squared length, not a length (Summer 2025 M8 Paper 2 Q12)

noteBlocks.lede: A cuboid has no triangle drawn on it, and that is the only difficulty. Every 3-D length or angle question hides a right-angled triangle inside the solid; find it, draw it on its own, and Pythagoras and SOHCAHTOA finish the job exactly as they did in two dimensions.
can: Pick the right-angled triangle out of a solid and draw it alone.
Find a space diagonal in two Pythagoras steps, or in one line.
Name the angle between a line and a plane in three letters.

noteBlocks.md: Think about the longest rod that will fit in a box, or the angle a guy rope makes with the ground. Neither is a length you can measure on one face. The trick is always the same: pick out a flat triangle inside the solid that has a right angle in it, redraw that triangle on its own with its letters and lengths, and then it is M2 and M3 work.

noteBlocks.caption: The whole topic in one picture: the triangle you need is inside the solid, and it is much easier to use once it is outside it.

noteBlocks.prompt: Warm-up, from M2. A rectangle measures 6 cm by 8 cm. How long is its diagonal, in cm?
noteBlocks.explain: $\sqrt{6^2 + 8^2} = \sqrt{100} = 10$ cm. Every 3-D question you meet starts with exactly this step, done inside the solid.

noteBlocks.text: Every 3-D question is a 2-D question in disguise

noteBlocks.md:
There is no new theorem here. Pythagoras and SOHCAHTOA still only work in a **right-angled triangle**, and a cuboid is full of them. The whole skill is finding the one triangle that contains what you want, and then drawing it again on its own, outside the solid, where the words opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse mean something.

Take the cuboid below. $AC$ lies flat in the base. $CG$ is vertical, so it is at right angles to **every** line in the base, including $AC$. That gives triangle $ACG$ a right angle at $C$.

noteBlocks.prompt: In the cuboid above, where is the right angle in triangle $ACG$?
noteBlocks.explain: $CG$ is vertical and $AC$ lies in the base, so they meet at right angles at $C$. That is why $AG$ is the hypotenuse of this triangle, and it is why the longest line in the whole cuboid is the space diagonal.

noteBlocks.md:
So the space diagonal comes out of **two Pythagoras steps joined at $AC$**:

1. In the base: $AC^2 = 8^2 + 6^2 = 100$, so $AC = 10$ cm.
2. Standing up: $AG^2 = AC^2 + CG^2 = 100 + 25 = 125$, so $AG = \sqrt{125} = 11.2$ cm (3 s.f.).

Substituting the first line into the second gives the one-line version, $AG^2 = a^2 + b^2 + c^2$. Both routes earn the same marks; the two-step version is safer because it leaves $AC$ written down, and you will need $AC$ again for the angle.

noteBlocks.prompt: A cuboid measures 2 cm by 3 cm by 6 cm. How long is its space diagonal, in cm?
noteBlocks.explain: $2^2 + 3^2 + 6^2 = 4 + 9 + 36 = 49$, and $\sqrt{49} = 7$ cm. Three dimensions, each squared, then one square root.

noteBlocks.title: Must know — none of this is on the formula sheet
noteBlocks.md:
$a^2 + b^2 = c^2$ and the three ratios $\sin$, $\cos$, $\tan$ are **not** printed on page 2. The sheet gives you the sine rule, the cosine rule, $\tfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$, the cone and the sphere, and nothing else that helps here.
**Space diagonal**: $d = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}$.
**Cube of edge $x$**: face diagonal $x\sqrt{2}$, space diagonal $x\sqrt{3}$.

noteBlocks.prompt: Fill the gap: to find a space diagonal you add the squares of ___ dimensions.
noteBlocks.explain: Three. Using only two gives the diagonal of a face, which is the most common way this question is started and not finished.

noteBlocks.text: The angle between a line and a plane

noteBlocks.md:
Here is the definition that settles every one of these questions.

**The angle between a line and a plane is the angle between the line and its shadow on that plane** — the shadow you would see with a light directly overhead.

Shine that light on the space diagonal $AG$. The shadow of $G$ lands on $C$, so the shadow of $AG$ is $AC$, and the angle you want is $\angle GAC$: between the diagonal and the base diagonal, measured at $A$.

noteBlocks.alt: Two copies of the same cuboid. In the left copy the base diagonal AC is dashed and the angle between the space diagonal AG and AC is marked at A: this is the angle between AG and the base. In the right copy the angle marked at A is between AG and the bottom front edge AB, labelled 'not this'.

noteBlocks.caption: The base is a whole plane, not one edge. The line the angle is measured from is the shadow of AG, which is the diagonal AC.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which three letters name the angle between $AG$ and the base $ABCD$?
noteBlocks.explain: $\angle GAB$ is measured from an edge, which is the mistake examiners saw most often in 2023 and 2025. $\angle AGC$ is at the top of the triangle, between $AG$ and the vertical edge, so it is $90°$ minus the angle you want.

noteBlocks.md:
Once the triangle is drawn on its own the trigonometry is M3 work. In triangle $ACG$ the side opposite $\angle GAC$ is the height $CG = 5$, and the side next to it is $AC = 10$, so $\tan \angle GAC = \dfrac{5}{10}$ and $\angle GAC = 26.6°$.

Choose **tangent** whenever you can: its two sides, the height and the base diagonal, are usually the exact ones. The hypotenuse $AG$ is often a root, and rounding it is where the last mark goes.

noteBlocks.prompt: A different cuboid has base diagonal $AC = 12$ cm and height $CG = 9$ cm. Find the angle between $AG$ and the base, in degrees, to 1 decimal place.
noteBlocks.explain: $\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{9}{12}\right) = 36.869\ldots = 36.9°$. Height on top, base diagonal underneath, every time.

noteBlocks.title: Why the shadow, and not some other line?
noteBlocks.md: Of all the lines you could draw in the base from $A$, the shadow $AC$ is the one that makes the **smallest** angle with $AG$. Tilt away from it, as $\angle GAB$ does, and the angle grows. The angle a line makes with a plane is defined as that smallest one, which is why there is only ever one right answer.

noteBlocks.prompt: The angle between a sloping line and a flat plane is measured to which line in the plane?
options: The line directly beneath it, its shadow
The nearest edge of the plane
Any line drawn from the foot of it
noteBlocks.answer: The line directly beneath it, its shadow
noteBlocks.explain: Drop the far end straight down on to the plane and join the two feet. That shadow gives the smallest angle, and that is the one meant.

noteBlocks.text: Pyramids: two angles, two different runs

noteBlocks.md:
A square-based pyramid gives CCEA two questions from one solid, and they have different answers.

**The slant edge $VA$ against the base.** The edge ends at a corner, so its shadow runs from the centre $M$ out to the corner $A$: that is **half a diagonal**.

noteBlocks.prompt: The pyramid above has base 10 cm and height 12 cm. For the angle between the **sloping face** and the base, what is the run along the base?
noteBlocks.explain: Half an edge, so $\tan z = \dfrac{12}{5}$ and $z = 67.4°$. Half a diagonal would have given the slant edge's angle, $59.5°$. Same pyramid, same height, two honest answers to two different questions.

noteBlocks.md:
The face is always the steeper of the two, because the same height stands over a shorter run. If your two answers come out the other way round, the runs have been swapped.

noteBlocks.explain: $G$ stands directly above $C$, so the shadow of $AG$ is $AC$, the diagonal of the base rectangle, and the angle is $\angle GAC$.

noteBlocks.md: **Cones** join the family through the slant height. The radius, the vertical height and the slant height make a right-angled triangle with the slant height as the hypotenuse, so $l^2 = r^2 + h^2$. The slant height is therefore always longer than the vertical height, which is worth checking before you use either in $\pi r l$.

noteBlocks.prompt: A cone has radius 7 cm and vertical height 24 cm. What is its slant height, in cm?
noteBlocks.explain: $\sqrt{7^2 + 24^2} = \sqrt{625} = 25$ cm. It is longer than 24, as it must be.

noteBlocks.text: Exact until the very last line

noteBlocks.md:
Here is a real cost. In the wedge above, $AC = \sqrt{97} = 9.8488\ldots$ m. The angle is $\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2.5}{AC}\right)$.

**Keeping $\sqrt{97}$:** 14.2°. **Rounding $AC$ to 9.8 first:** 14.3°. **Rounding to 10:** 14.0°.

noteBlocks.prompt: Complete the sentence an examiner wants to see first: the angle between $AG$ and the base is angle ___ .
noteBlocks.explain: Three letters, with the vertex of the angle in the middle. Writing that line before any calculation is worth a mark on its own.

noteBlocks.md: All three look like sensible answers on the page, and only the first earns the accuracy mark. Mark schemes print the long decimal ($14.242943\ldots$) precisely because that is what an unrounded chain produces.

noteBlocks.prompt: You have $AC^2 = 97$ and need the angle. What do you type in?
options: $\sqrt{97}$, and round once at the end
noteBlocks.answer: $\sqrt{97}$, and round once at the end
noteBlocks.explain: 97 is exact but it is $AC^2$, not a length. Use the root for the ratio, keep the 97 for any further Pythagoras step, and round only on the answer line.

noteBlocks.prompt: A cube has space diagonal 12 cm. Write $x^2$ as a number, where $x$ cm is an edge.
noteBlocks.explain: $3x^2 = 144$, so $x^2 = 48$ and $x = \sqrt{48} = 4\sqrt{3}$ cm. Backwards questions are the same rule, solved for the edge instead.

noteBlocks.title: Pythagoras and Trigonometry in 3D
noteBlocks.why: A Northern Ireland teacher working CCEA-style 3-D questions, including the wording CCEA uses for the angle with the base. Useful once you have done a few yourself.

noteBlocks.prompt: Last one. A cuboid is 5 cm by 12 cm by 9 cm. Find the angle between its space diagonal and the base, in degrees, to 1 decimal place.
noteBlocks.explain: $AC = \sqrt{5^2 + 12^2} = 13$, then $\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{9}{13}\right) = 34.695\ldots = 34.7°$. Two lines, once you know which triangle to draw.

noteBlocks.md: **It is learnable.** Over half the entry gained full marks on the angle between a space diagonal and the base, and nearly everyone made a sensible start. Examiners put that down to preparation, which is exactly what this page is for.

noteBlocks.prompt: A question asks for the angle between $AG$ and **the largest face**, rather than the base. What changes?
options: Use the diagonal of that face, and the edge perpendicular to it
Nothing, the answer is the same as with the base
Use the longest edge of the cuboid
noteBlocks.answer: Use the diagonal of that face, and the edge perpendicular to it
noteBlocks.explain: The plane has moved, so the shadow moves with it. For a $9 \times 12$ face, the shadow is that face's diagonal, 15, and the perpendicular distance is the remaining edge. The method is identical once you have asked which plane.

noteBlocks.prompt: Which of these would an examiner reward first in a 3-mark angle question?
options: Naming the angle, or drawing the triangle with its lengths on it
Writing the final answer to 3 significant figures
noteBlocks.answer: Naming the angle, or drawing the triangle with its lengths on it
noteBlocks.explain: CCEA schemes for this topic open with a mark for using or identifying the correct angle, before any ratio appears. It is the cheapest mark in the question and the one most often left behind.

noteBlocks.md:
Pick the right-angled triangle out of a solid and draw it alone.
Find a space diagonal in two Pythagoras steps, or in one line.
Name the angle between a line and a plane in three letters.
Tell a face angle from an edge angle on a pyramid.
Keep values exact until the final line.

Four or five marks, late in the paper: a space diagonal, then the angle it makes with the base. The first mark is the base diagonal; the last is the angle to the accuracy named. Stuck: redraw the right-angled triangle on its own beside the working and label its three sides.

noteBlocks.title: Not on this spec
noteBlocks.md: 3-D coordinates and 3-D vectors; the angle between two planes other than a face and the base; anything needing the cosine rule **in this topic** (a non-right triangle inside a solid belongs to the sine and cosine rule topic, and CCEA has set it that way, as in the November 2021 cuboid where the angle asked for sat at the far corner); surface areas or volumes, which live in the mensuration topics.

resources: Formula sheet printed on page 2 of the paper

workedExamples.stem:
$ABCDEFGH$ is a cuboid. $AB = 8$ cm, $BC = 6$ cm and $CG = 5$ cm.

(a) Show that $AC = 10$ cm.
(b) Calculate the length of the space diagonal $AG$.
(c) Calculate the angle between $AG$ and the base $ABCD$.

The base diagonal AC is dashed and the space diagonal AG is drawn thick, with the angle x between them marked at A and a right angle marked at C. On the right, triangle ACG is drawn again on its own: AC = 10 cm along the bottom, CG = 5 cm vertical, AG as the hypotenuse and the angle x at A.

steps.working:
Triangle $ABC$ lies flat in the base, right-angled at $B$.
$AC^2 = 8^2 + 6^2 = 64 + 36 = 100$
steps.decision: Nothing in three dimensions can be done until you have found a triangle that is right-angled and whose sides you know. The base is a rectangle, so $ABC$ has a right angle at $B$, and two of its sides are printed on the diagram. That is the triangle to start in.

options: Because $ABC$ is right-angled at $B$ and two of its sides are given
Because $AC$ is the longest line in the cuboid
Because the base is the biggest face
whyMenu.explain: The longest line in the cuboid is the space diagonal $AG$, not $AC$, and the size of a face never decides anything. What makes $ABC$ usable is the right angle at $B$ with two known sides.

steps.decision: A show-that part needs the printed answer to appear at the end of your working, so write the square root line out. Stopping at $AC^2 = 100$ leaves the second mark unearned, because 100 is not a length.

steps.working:
Triangle $ACG$ stands vertically, right-angled at $C$ because $CG$ is vertical and $AC$ is in the base.
$AG^2 = AC^2 + CG^2 = 10^2 + 5^2 = 125$
steps.decision: Now use the answer from part (a) as one side of a new triangle. $CG$ is vertical, so it is at right angles to every line in the base, including $AC$. Draw that triangle beside the solid before you write anything: the whole of 3-D Pythagoras is two 2-D steps joined at $AC$.

Keep $\sqrt{125}$ on the calculator for part (c); write the rounded 11.2 on the answer line only. In one line you could have written $AG^2 = 8^2 + 6^2 + 5^2$, which is the same two steps rolled together.

steps.working: The angle between $AG$ and the base is $\angle GAC$.
steps.decision: The shadow of $AG$ on the base is $AC$, so the angle you want sits between the diagonal and its shadow, at $A$. Write the three letters down; examiners give a mark for naming or marking the angle before any trigonometry happens, and it is the mark most candidates miss.

whyMenu.explain: $\angle GAB$ is the angle between $AG$ and one edge of the base, not between $AG$ and the base itself. $\angle AGC$ is at the top of the triangle, so it is the angle $AG$ makes with the vertical edge; it comes to $90°$ minus the angle you were asked for.

steps.working:
In triangle $ACG$: opposite $= CG = 5$, adjacent $= AC = 10$.
$\tan \angle GAC = \dfrac{5}{10}$
steps.decision: In the extracted triangle the labels are obvious: $CG$ is opposite the angle, $AC$ is next to it, so the ratio is tangent. Tangent is also the safer choice here because both of its sides are exact whole numbers, while the hypotenuse is a root.
Round once, at the end. A CCEA answer line for an angle prints the degree symbol, so a value to one decimal place or to three significant figures is what the scheme expects.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: $AC = 10$ cm, $AG = \sqrt{125} = 11.2$ cm (3 s.f.) and the angle between $AG$ and the base is $26.6°$

$VABCD$ is a pyramid with a square base of side 10 cm. The apex $V$ is vertically above the centre $M$ of the base, and $VM = 12$ cm.

(a) Calculate the length of the slant edge $VA$.
(b) Calculate the angle between $VA$ and the base.
(c) $N$ is the midpoint of $AB$. Calculate the angle between the sloping face $VAB$ and the base.

figure.alt: On the left, a square-based pyramid VABCD drawn in oblique projection, base edge AB = 10 cm, with the hidden edges AD, DC and VD dashed. The base diagonal AC is dashed, the vertical height VM from the apex to the centre M of the base is dashed and labelled 12 cm, and the slant edge VA is drawn thick with the angle y marked at A. On the right, triangle AMV is drawn on its own: AM = 7.07 cm along the bottom, VM = 12 cm vertical, VA as the hypotenuse and the angle y at A.

steps.decision: $V$ is above the centre of the base, so the foot of the height is $M$, the point where the diagonals cross. To reach $M$ from $A$ you travel half of a diagonal, and the diagonal comes from Pythagoras in the square base.

steps.working:
Triangle $AMV$ is right-angled at $M$.
$VA^2 = AM^2 + VM^2 = 50 + 144 = 194$, so $VA = \sqrt{194} = 13.928\ldots = 13.9$ cm (3 s.f.)
steps.decision: $AM^2$ is exactly 50, because $AM = \tfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{200}$ and squaring undoes the root: there is no need to square a rounded 7.07. Keeping the exact 50 is what protects the accuracy mark in part (b).

whyMenu.explain: $AM = \tfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{200}$, so $AM^2 = \tfrac{1}{4} \times 200 = 50$. Squaring the rounded 7.07 gives 49.98, and that small drift is exactly how accuracy marks disappear.

steps.working:
The angle between $VA$ and the base is $\angle VAM$ (that is, $\angle VAC$).
$\tan \angle VAM = \dfrac{12}{7.0710\ldots}$, so $\angle VAM = 59.49\ldots° = 59.5°$ (1 d.p.)
steps.decision: The shadow of the slant edge $VA$ on the base is $AM$, along the diagonal, so the angle sits at $A$ in triangle $AMV$. Type the $\sqrt{50}$ straight into the calculator rather than 7.07.

steps.working:
For the face $VAB$: $N$ is the midpoint of $AB$, so $MN = 5$ cm and $VN \perp AB$.
$\tan \angle VNM = \dfrac{12}{5}$, so $\angle VNM = 67.38\ldots° = 67.4°$ (1 d.p.)
steps.decision: A face is not a line, so the angle is measured along the line of greatest slope: drop from $V$ to the midpoint $N$ of the bottom edge. The shadow of $VN$ on the base is $MN$, which is half the base edge, 5 cm, and not half the diagonal. Two different angles come out of the same pyramid, which is why the question can ask for either.

options: $MN = 5$ cm, half of a base edge
whyMenu.explain: Half the diagonal takes you from the centre out to a corner, which is the slant-edge question. Half an edge takes you from the centre to the middle of a side, which is the face question. Naming the point $N$ on your own sketch keeps the two apart.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: $VA = \sqrt{194} = 13.9$ cm (3 s.f.); the slant edge meets the base at $59.5°$; the sloping face meets the base at $67.4°$

Hidden edges AD, DC and DH are dashed. The base diagonal AC is dashed and the sloping line AG is drawn thick, with the angle theta marked at A and a right angle at C. On the right, triangle ACG on its own: AC = root 97 m along the bottom, CG = 2.5 m vertical, AG the hypotenuse, angle theta at A.

steps.working:
In the base, $ABC$ is right-angled at $B$.
$AC^2 = 9^2 + 4^2 = 97$, so $AC = \sqrt{97} = 9.8488\ldots$ m
steps.decision: The solid is not a cuboid, but the method does not change: find the shadow first. $AC$ is the shadow of $AG$ on the ground, and it comes from the rectangle you are standing on.
Use $AC^2 = 97$, not $9.8488^2$. Squaring a square root hands back the whole number, so the second Pythagoras step stays exact and quick.

steps.working:
The angle with the base is $\angle GAC$.
$\tan \angle GAC = \dfrac{2.5}{\sqrt{97}}$
steps.decision: Type the root itself into the calculator. It is one keystroke more than typing 9.8, and it is the difference between the answer the scheme prints and an answer that is out by a tenth of a degree.

steps.working:
$\angle GAC = 14.2429\ldots° = 14.2°$ (1 d.p.)
Rounding $AC$ to 9.8 first would have given $14.3°$ instead.
steps.decision: Both versions look reasonable on the page, and only one of them earns the accuracy mark. This is the single most common way a correct method still loses its last mark in this topic.

options: Keep $\sqrt{97}$ and round once at the end
Round $AC$ to 9.8, then find the angle
Round $AC$ to 10, then find the angle
whyMenu.explain: Rounding to 9.8 gives 14.3° and rounding to 10 gives 14.0°, so both miss 14.2°. Keep the root, or use your calculator's answer key, and round only on the answer line.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: $AG = \sqrt{103.25} = 10.2$ m (3 s.f.) and $AG$ makes an angle of $14.2°$ with the base

steps.working:
Let each edge be $x$ cm. The three dimensions are $x$, $x$ and $x$.
$x^2 + x^2 + x^2 = 12^2$
steps.decision: Read the space-diagonal rule backwards. The sum of the squares of the three dimensions is the square of the diagonal, whichever of the four quantities is the unknown one.
Collect the three identical squares first. Dividing by 3 before taking any root keeps the arithmetic in whole numbers, which matters on the paper where the calculator is away.

whyMenu.explain: $x^2 + x^2 + x^2$ is $3x^2$, not $3x$: it is three copies of the square. And 144 is being shared between the three squares, so it is divided by 3, not multiplied.

steps.decision: The form $a\sqrt{b}$ is being asked for, so pull out the largest square factor: 16 divides 48 and $\sqrt{16} = 4$. Leaving $\sqrt{48}$ would not be in the form demanded, and a decimal would earn nothing on this paper.

169 is $AG^2$. A squared length is not a length: take the square root to finish, giving 13 cm.

options.feedback: The shadow of $AG$ on the base is $AC$, and the angle between a line and a plane is the angle between the line and its shadow.
$AB$ is one edge of the base, not the shadow of $AG$. This is the answer examiners saw most often in Summer 2025, and it gives an angle that is too large.
That angle is at the top of the triangle, between $AG$ and the vertical edge $CG$. It comes to $90°$ minus the angle asked for, so subtracting from 90 would rescue it.
Draw triangle $ACG$ on its own and you can see $\angle ACG$ is the right angle, always $90°$. Sketching the triangle separately is what makes this obvious.

items.stem: In the vertical triangle $ACG$, $AC = 10$ and $CG = 6$, and the right angle is at $C$. Which line finds the angle at $A$?
items.skill: Choose the ratio inside the extracted triangle

options.feedback: Opposite over adjacent, and both of those sides are known exactly, so nothing has to be worked out first.
The fraction is upside down: 6 is opposite the angle at $A$ and 10 is beside it. This gives $59.0°$ instead of $31.0°$, and the two add to $90°$, which is a useful check.
Sine needs the hypotenuse underneath, and here 10 is the adjacent side. The hypotenuse of this triangle is $AG$, which has not been found yet.
Cosine is adjacent over hypotenuse. Here 6 is the opposite side, so this ratio pairs the wrong two sides.

items.stem: A pyramid has a square base of side 12 cm and a vertical height of 9 cm. For the angle between the **slant edge** and the base, which length do you need along the base?
items.skill: Half the diagonal for a slant edge, half the edge for a face

options.feedback: The slant edge ends at a corner, and the shadow from the centre to a corner is half a diagonal.
Half the edge takes you from the centre to the middle of a side, which is the sloping-face question. This mix-up gives $56.3°$ instead of $46.7°$.
The apex stands above the centre, so the horizontal run from a corner is only as far as the centre: half of the diagonal.

options.text: No base length is needed, the height is enough
options.feedback: One length cannot fix an angle. Draw the right-angled triangle on its own and it has two sides you must know before any ratio can be written.

items.stem: For this pyramid, the angle $z$ between the sloping face $VAB$ and the base is found from which right-angled triangle?
items.skill: Use the perpendicular height and half the base for a face angle

options.feedback: $VN$ is the line of greatest slope on that face, its shadow is $MN$, and $MN$ is half the base edge.
That triangle contains the slant edge $VA$, so it answers the slant-edge question. For a face, go to the middle of the bottom edge, not to a corner.
Triangle $VAB$ is the sloping face itself, and it has no right angle in it. The angle you want is between that face and the floor, so the triangle must have one line in the face and one in the base.
$MB$ also runs to a corner, so this is the slant-edge triangle again, drawn from the other end of the edge.

items.stem: A cone has base radius 7 cm and vertical height 24 cm. Which statement is right?
items.skill: Tell the slant height apart from the vertical height

options.text: The slant height is 25 cm, from $\sqrt{7^2 + 24^2}$
options.feedback: Radius, vertical height and slant height make a right-angled triangle, with the slant height as the hypotenuse.

options.text: The slant height is 24 cm, the same as the vertical height
options.feedback: The vertical height goes straight down the middle; the slant height runs down the surface to the rim, so it is always the longer of the two.
Subtracting treats 24 as the hypotenuse. The hypotenuse is the side opposite the right angle, and the right angle is where the height meets the base, so the slant height is the hypotenuse.
Lengths are added along a path, never across a triangle. Pythagoras adds the squares.

items.stem: You have found $AC = \sqrt{97}$ and need $\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2.5}{AC}\right)$. Which keeps the accuracy mark?
items.skill: Work with exact values until the final line

options.text: Type $\sqrt{97}$ into the calculator and round once at the end
options.feedback: One rounding, on the answer line. That is what the mark scheme's long decimal is telling you to do.

options.text: Round $AC$ to 9.8, then find the angle
options.feedback: This gives 14.3° instead of 14.2°. The method mark survives, the accuracy mark does not.

options.text: Round $AC$ to 10, then find the angle
options.feedback: Rounding to a whole number moves the answer to 14.0°, which is out by a third of a degree.

options.text: Use 97 rather than $\sqrt{97}$, since 97 is exact
options.feedback: 97 is exact but it is an area, not a length: it is $AC^2$. Keep the root for any ratio, and keep the 97 for any further Pythagoras step.

items.stem: The space diagonal of a cube is 9 cm. Which equation starts the problem correctly?

options.feedback: Three equal squares add to the square of the diagonal, so $x^2 = 27$ and $x = 3\sqrt{3}$ cm.
Two squares give a face diagonal. A space diagonal crosses all three dimensions, so three squares are added.
The edges are not simply shared out along the diagonal; it is the squares that add, not the lengths.
The first line is right and then the root is missing: $x = \sqrt{27} = 3\sqrt{3} = 5.196\ldots$ cm.

parts.stem:
$ABCDEFGH$ is a cuboid with $AB = 8$ cm, $BC = 15$ cm and $CG = 6$ cm.
Calculate the length of the base diagonal $AC$.
hints: The base $ABCD$ is a rectangle, so triangle $ABC$ has a right angle at $B$.
Only two of the three dimensions belong in this calculation.
$64 + 225 = 289$, and 289 is a square number.
parts.workedSolution: Triangle $ABC$ lies in the base and is right-angled at $B$, so $AC^2 = 8^2 + 15^2 = 64 + 225 = 289$ and $AC = \sqrt{289} = 17$ cm.

commonErrors.feedback: The two lengths were added rather than their squares. Pythagoras adds the squares and then takes the root: $\sqrt{64 + 225} = 17$ cm, which is sensibly shorter than going 8 cm then 15 cm round the edges.
289 is $AC^2$. One more keystroke gives the length itself, $\sqrt{289} = 17$ cm.

resources: Formula sheet printed on page 2 of the paper

parts.stem:
$ABCDEFGH$ is a cuboid with $AB = 4$ cm, $BC = 4$ cm and $CG = 7$ cm.
Calculate the length of the space diagonal $AG$.
hints: All three dimensions go in, each one squared.
In two steps: the base diagonal squared is $4^2 + 4^2 = 32$, then add $7^2$.

commonErrors.feedback: This is $AC$, the diagonal of the base: only two dimensions were used. Adding $7^2$ to the 32 you already have finishes it, and $AG = 9$ cm.
The three lengths were added. A straight line through the inside of the box is shorter than a walk along three edges, so add the squares instead.

parts.stem:
$ABCDEFGH$ is a cuboid with $AB = 6$ cm, $BC = 8$ cm and $CG = 7$ cm.
Write down, in three letters, the angle that $AG$ makes with the base $ABCD$.

scheme.for: $\angle GAC$ (accept $\angle CAG$, or the angle marked on the diagram at $A$ between $AG$ and $AC$)

hints: Shine a light straight down on $AG$: the shadow it casts on the base is the line the angle is measured from.
That shadow is the base diagonal, not an edge.
parts.workedSolution: The projection of $AG$ on the base is $AC$, so the angle between $AG$ and the base is $\angle GAC$.

commonErrors.feedback: $\angle GAB$ is measured from the edge $AB$. The base is a whole plane, and the line to measure from is the shadow of $AG$, which is the diagonal $AC$.
$\angle AGC$ sits at the top, between $AG$ and the vertical edge. It is $90°$ minus the angle you want, so this answer can be rescued by subtracting from 90.

parts.stem: Calculate the size of this angle.

scheme.for: $AC = 10$ seen, or triangle $ACG$ drawn with two known sides

hints: Find $AC$ first: it is the diagonal of a 6 by 8 rectangle.
In triangle $ACG$ the height 7 is opposite the angle and $AC$ is next to it.
parts.workedSolution: $AC = \sqrt{6^2 + 8^2} = 10$ cm. In triangle $ACG$, right-angled at $C$, $\tan \angle GAC = \dfrac{7}{10}$, so $\angle GAC = 34.992\ldots = 35.0°$.

commonErrors.feedback: The 6 cm edge has been used instead of the base diagonal, which measures the angle from $AB$ rather than from the base. Replace the 6 with $AC = 10$.
This is the angle at $G$, between $AG$ and the vertical edge. Subtract from $90°$ to get 35.0°, or work from $A$ in the first place.

parts.stem:
$ABCDEFGH$ is a cuboid with $AB = 9$ cm, $BC = 12$ cm and $CG = 4$ cm.
Calculate the angle between $AG$ and one of the two largest faces.

scheme.for: Largest face identified as $9 \times 12$ and its diagonal found: $\sqrt{9^2 + 12^2} = 15$

hints: Compare the three faces: $9 \times 12$, $9 \times 4$ and $12 \times 4$. The largest is the base.
The line you measure from is the diagonal of that face, and the perpendicular distance from $G$ to it is the remaining edge, 4 cm.
$\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{4}{15}\right) = 14.93\ldots$
parts.workedSolution: The largest faces are the $9 \times 12$ rectangles, and $ABCD$ is one of them. Its diagonal is $AC = \sqrt{9^2 + 12^2} = 15$ cm, and $G$ stands 4 cm above $C$, so $\tan(\text{angle}) = \dfrac{4}{15}$ and the angle is $14.9°$.

commonErrors.feedback: This is an angle inside the face itself, between the diagonal and an edge. The question wants the angle that $AG$ makes with the face, which needs the 4 cm standing perpendicular to it.
15 cm is the diagonal of the largest face, so the first mark is safe. The question asks for an angle, so one more step is needed: $\tan^{-1}(4 \div 15)$.

questions.solutionProgram: largest face is 9 by 12; its diagonal = sqrt(81+144) = 15; tan angle = 4/15; angle = 14.9314174..., 3sf 14.9

parts.stem:
$VABCD$ is a pyramid with a square base of side 8 cm. The apex $V$ is vertically above the centre $M$ of the base and $VM = 15$ cm.
Calculate the length of the slant edge $VA$.
hints: $M$ is where the diagonals cross, so $AM$ is half of the base diagonal.
Half of $\sqrt{128}$ squares to 32, so there is no need for a decimal here.

commonErrors.feedback: Half a base edge (4 cm) was used. That run belongs to the sloping face; the slant edge runs out to a corner, so the run is half the diagonal, whose square is 32.
The whole diagonal was used. The apex stands above the centre, so the horizontal distance from $A$ to the foot of the height is only half of $AC$.

parts.stem: Calculate the angle between $VA$ and the base.

scheme.for: Angle $VAM$ (or $VAC$) identified, or triangle $AMV$ drawn separately

hints: The shadow of $VA$ on the base is $AM$.
Use the exact $\sqrt{32}$, not a rounded 5.66.
$\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{15}{\sqrt{32}}\right) = 69.3\ldots$
parts.workedSolution: The angle is $\angle VAM$. $\tan \angle VAM = \dfrac{15}{\sqrt{32}}$, so $\angle VAM = 69.3374\ldots = 69.3°$.

commonErrors.feedback: This is the angle at $V$, between the slant edge and the vertical height. Subtracting from $90°$ gives 69.3°.
Half the base edge has been used again. For a slant edge the run along the base is half the diagonal, $\sqrt{32} = 5.66$ cm, not 4 cm.

parts.stem:
$VABCD$ is a pyramid with a square base of side 12 cm. The apex $V$ is 9 cm vertically above the centre $M$ of the base, and $N$ is the midpoint of $AB$.
Calculate the angle between the sloping face $VAB$ and the base.

scheme.for: $MN = 6$ used (half of a base edge), or triangle $NMV$ drawn separately
$\tan \angle VNM = \dfrac{9}{6}$ (or $\tan$ of the same ratio from $VN = \sqrt{117}$)

hints: A face meets the base along the line $AB$; the steepest line in the face runs from $V$ down to the midpoint $N$.
The shadow of $VN$ on the base is $MN$, half of a base edge.
parts.workedSolution: $N$ is the midpoint of $AB$, so $MN = 6$ cm and $VN$ is perpendicular to $AB$. In triangle $NMV$, right-angled at $M$, $\tan \angle VNM = \dfrac{9}{6} = 1.5$, so the angle is $56.3°$.

commonErrors.feedback: Half the diagonal (8.49 cm) was used, which gives the angle the slant edge makes with the base, 46.7°. For a face use half an edge, 6 cm.
The whole base edge, 12 cm, was used as the run. Draw triangle $NMV$ on its own and the run is clearly $MN$, from the centre to the midpoint of the edge.

parts.stem:
A cone has base radius 7 cm and vertical height 24 cm. $V$ is the apex, $O$ is the centre of the base and $P$ is a point on the edge of the base.
Show that the slant height $VP$ is 25 cm.
hints: The height meets the base at right angles, so $OP$, $OV$ and $VP$ make a right-angled triangle.
The slant height is the hypotenuse of that triangle.
parts.workedSolution: $OV$ is perpendicular to the base, so triangle $POV$ is right-angled at $O$ with the slant height as hypotenuse: $VP^2 = 7^2 + 24^2 = 49 + 576 = 625$, so $VP = 25$ cm.

commonErrors.feedback: Subtracting treats the 24 as the hypotenuse. The right angle is where the height meets the base, so the side opposite it, the slant height, is the longest and the squares are added.
625 is $VP^2$. A show-that part needs the final line to be the printed length, so take the root: $VP = 25$ cm.

parts.stem: Calculate the angle between the slant height $VP$ and the base.
hints: The angle sits at $P$, where the slant height meets the base.
$\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{24}{7}\right) = 73.7\ldots$
parts.workedSolution: In triangle $POV$, $\tan \angle VPO = \dfrac{24}{7}$, so the angle is $73.7°$. With the 25 from part (a), $\cos \angle VPO = \dfrac{7}{25}$ gives the same value.

commonErrors.feedback: 16.3° is the angle at the apex, between the slant height and the vertical. The angle with the base is its complement, 73.7°.

parts.stem:
A wedge-shaped ramp has a horizontal base $ABCD$ with $AB = 8$ m and $BC = 6$ m. The back face $DCGH$ is vertical with $CG = 3$ m, and $ABGH$ is the sloping surface.
Calculate the angle that $AG$ makes with the base.
hints: The solid is not a cuboid, and the method does not change: find the shadow of $AG$ on the ground first.
$G$ stands 3 m above $C$.
parts.workedSolution: $AC = \sqrt{8^2 + 6^2} = 10$ m is the shadow of $AG$ on the base. In triangle $ACG$, right-angled at $C$, $\tan \angle GAC = \dfrac{3}{10}$, so the angle is $16.7°$.

commonErrors.feedback: The 8 m edge was used instead of the base diagonal. That is the angle the sloping face makes with the base along $AH$, not the angle $AG$ makes with the base.
The 6 m edge was used as the run. Redraw triangle $ACG$ on its own: the side next to the angle is the base diagonal $AC$, which is 10 m.

parts.stem:
A crate is a cuboid $ABCDEFGH$ with $AB = 1.3$ m, $BC = 90$ cm and $CG = 0.5$ m.
Calculate the length of the longest straight rod that will fit inside the crate. Give your answer in centimetres, correct to 3 significant figures.

scheme.for: All three lengths in the same unit: 130, 90 and 50 (cm)

hints: Convert everything to centimetres before any squaring: 1.3 m is 130 cm.
The longest straight line inside a cuboid is the space diagonal.
parts.workedSolution: In centimetres the crate is $130 \times 90 \times 50$. The longest straight line inside is the space diagonal: $AG^2 = 130^2 + 90^2 + 50^2 = 16\,900 + 8\,100 + 2\,500 = 27\,500$, so $AG = \sqrt{27\,500} = 165.8\ldots = 166$ cm (3 s.f.).

commonErrors.feedback: Metres and centimetres went into the same calculation, so the 90 swamped the other two. Convert first: 1.3 m is 130 cm and 0.5 m is 50 cm.
158 cm is the diagonal across the floor of the crate. The rod can also be tilted upwards, so the 50 cm height belongs in the calculation too.

parts.stem: A rod is 1.6 m long. Explain whether it will fit inside the crate.

accepted: Yes, because 160 cm is less than 165.8 cm
Yes, 1.6 m is shorter than the space diagonal

scheme.for: Yes, with a comparison: $160 < 165.8$ (follow through from part (a))
scheme.examinerNote: A bare yes with no comparison scores nothing; the reason is the mark.

hints: Put both lengths in the same unit before comparing.
The rod must lie along the longest line available, the space diagonal.
parts.workedSolution: The rod is 160 cm and the longest line inside the crate is 165.8 cm, so the rod fits, but only if it is placed along the space diagonal.

commonErrors.feedback: 1.6 m is 160 cm, which is shorter than the 166 cm diagonal, so it does fit. Comparing 1.6 with 166 without converting is what turns this answer around.

parts.stem:
The space diagonal of a cube is 20 cm.
Calculate the length of an edge of the cube, correct to 3 significant figures.
hints: Call the edge $x$ and write the space-diagonal rule with all three dimensions equal.
$x^2 + x^2 + x^2$ collects to $3x^2$.
Divide by 3 before taking the square root.
parts.workedSolution: Let the edge be $x$ cm. Then $3x^2 = 20^2 = 400$, so $x^2 = \dfrac{400}{3} = 133.33\ldots$ and $x = 11.547\ldots = 11.5$ cm (3 s.f.).

commonErrors.feedback: Dividing the diagonal by 3 treats the three edges as sections of it. They are not: it is the three squares that add to $20^2$, so $3x^2 = 400$.
Two squares were used, which is the rule for a face diagonal. A space diagonal uses all three, so divide 400 by 3 rather than by 2.

parts.stem:
$ABCDEFGH$ is a cuboid with $AB = 9$ cm and $BC = 12$ cm. The space diagonal $AG$ makes an angle of $40°$ with the base.
Show that the base diagonal $AC$ is 15 cm.
hints: The base is a rectangle, so triangle $ABC$ is right-angled at $B$.

commonErrors.feedback: 225 is $AC^2$, and a show-that part must finish on the printed length: $\sqrt{225} = 15$ cm.

parts.stem: Calculate the height $CG$ of the cuboid.

scheme.for: Triangle $ACG$ used with the $40°$ at $A$ and $AC = 15$

hints: The $40°$ lives in triangle $ACG$, between $AG$ and $AC$.
$CG$ is opposite the angle and $AC$ is next to it, so tangent again.
Multiply, do not divide: $CG = 15 \times \tan 40°$.
parts.workedSolution: In triangle $ACG$, right-angled at $C$, $\tan 40° = \dfrac{CG}{15}$, so $CG = 15\tan 40° = 12.5865\ldots = 12.6$ cm (3 s.f.).

commonErrors.feedback: The ratio was rearranged the wrong way round: $\tan 40° = \dfrac{CG}{15}$ means $CG = 15\tan 40°$, so the 15 multiplies. Dividing gives a height taller than the base diagonal, which the diagram rules out.
The 12 cm edge was used instead of $AC$. The $40°$ is measured from the base diagonal, so the triangle containing it has $AC = 15$ along the bottom.

parts.stem:
$ABCDEFGH$ is a cuboid with $AB = 6$ cm, $BC = 6$ cm and $CG = 12$ cm.
Find the length of $AG$, leaving your answer in the form $a\sqrt{b}$.
hints: There is no calculator, so leave the root alone until the end.
Look for the largest square factor of 216: it is 36.

commonErrors.feedback: $\sqrt{216}$ is correct but not in the form asked for. Split off the largest square factor: $216 = 36 \times 6$, so the answer is $6\sqrt{6}$.
$6\sqrt{2}$ is the diagonal of the square base, from two dimensions. The 12 cm height still has to be added in as $12^2$.

$ABCDEFGH$ is a cuboid with $AB = 5$ cm, $BC = 12$ cm and $CG = 9$ cm.
Show that $AC = 13$ cm.
hints: Triangle $ABC$ lies flat in the base and is right-angled at $B$.
$25 + 144 = 169$, and 169 is a square number.

commonErrors.feedback: 169 is $AC^2$. Show-that parts are marked on the final line, so write $AC = \sqrt{169} = 13$ cm.

parts.stem: Calculate the length of the space diagonal $AG$.
hints: Use part (a): triangle $ACG$ is right-angled at $C$ with $AC = 13$ and $CG = 9$.

commonErrors.feedback: 15 cm is the diagonal of the $12 \times 9$ face. The space diagonal needs the third dimension as well, so start from $AC = 13$ and add $9^2$.

parts.stem: Calculate the angle between $AG$ and the base $ABCD$.

scheme.for: $\angle GAC$ identified, or triangle $ACG$ drawn separately with $AC$ and $CG$ marked

hints: Name the angle before calculating: the shadow of $AG$ on the base is $AC$.
The exact sides are 9 and 13, so tangent keeps everything exact.
$\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{9}{13}\right) = 34.69\ldots$
parts.workedSolution: The angle between $AG$ and the base is $\angle GAC$. In triangle $ACG$, $\tan \angle GAC = \dfrac{9}{13}$, so $\angle GAC = 34.6952\ldots = 34.7°$ (1 d.p.).

commonErrors.feedback: The 5 cm edge was used, so this is $\angle GAB$ rather than the angle with the base. Less than half of the Summer 2025 entry identified this angle, and naming it in three letters first is what fixes it.

15.8 is the hypotenuse of the 2-D triangle, so it cannot sit under the 9 in a tangent ratio: tangent needs the adjacent side, 13, and tan⁻¹(9 ÷ 13) gives 34.7°. Using the hypotenuse with tangent gives 29.7°, which is not an angle in this triangle. If you prefer sine, keep the exact √250 as the hypotenuse.

parts.stem:
$VABCD$ is a pyramid with a square base of side 16 cm. The apex $V$ is vertically above the centre $M$ of the base, and the slant edge $VA$ is 17 cm.
Show that the vertical height of the pyramid is 12.7 cm, correct to 3 significant figures.
hints: The height drops to the centre of the base, so the triangle is $AMV$ with $AM$ half a diagonal.
This time the hypotenuse is known, so the squares are subtracted.
parts.workedSolution: $AC = \sqrt{16^2 + 16^2} = \sqrt{512}$, so $AM = \tfrac{1}{2}\sqrt{512}$ and $AM^2 = 128$. In triangle $AMV$, right-angled at $M$, $VM^2 = VA^2 - AM^2 = 289 - 128 = 161$, so $VM = \sqrt{161} = 12.688\ldots = 12.7$ cm (3 s.f.).

commonErrors.feedback: The squares were added, which treats $VA$ as a shorter side. $VA$ is the hypotenuse of triangle $AMV$ because the right angle is at $M$, so subtract: $17^2 - 128$.
Half a base edge (8 cm) was used. The slant edge $VA$ runs to a corner, so the horizontal run is half a diagonal, whose square is 128 rather than 64.

parts.stem: $N$ is the midpoint of $AB$. Calculate the angle between the sloping face $VAB$ and the base.
hints: The line of greatest slope in the face runs from $V$ to $N$, and its shadow is $MN$.
$MN$ is half of a base edge, so 8 cm.
Keep $\sqrt{161}$ rather than 12.7.
parts.workedSolution: In triangle $NMV$, right-angled at $M$, $\tan \angle VNM = \dfrac{\sqrt{161}}{8}$, so $\angle VNM = 57.769\ldots = 57.8°$. (The slant height $VN = \sqrt{161 + 64} = 15$ cm, a useful check.)

commonErrors.feedback: Half the diagonal was used, giving the angle the slant edge makes with the base, 48.3°. The face is the steeper of the two at 57.8°.

parts.stem:
A loading bay is a wedge. Its horizontal base $ABCD$ has $AB = 15$ m and $BC = 8$ m, the back face $DCGH$ is vertical with $CG = 4.5$ m, and $ABGH$ is the sloping surface.
Calculate the length of $AG$.
hints: Find the diagonal of the base first: 15 and 8 make a 17.

commonErrors.feedback: 17 m is $AC$, the diagonal across the ground. $G$ is 4.5 m above $C$, so one more Pythagoras step is needed.

parts.stem: Calculate the angle that $AG$ makes with the base.

scheme.for: $\angle GAC$ identified, or triangle $ACG$ drawn separately

hints: The shadow of $AG$ on the ground is $AC$, so the angle is at $A$ in triangle $ACG$.
Both exact sides are known: 4.5 and 17.
$\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{4.5}{17}\right) = 14.8\ldots$
parts.workedSolution: The angle is $\angle GAC$. $\tan \angle GAC = \dfrac{4.5}{17}$, so $\angle GAC = 14.8265\ldots = 14.8°$ (1 d.p.).

commonErrors.feedback: The 15 m edge was used instead of $AC$. That is the slope you would climb walking straight up the side $AH$, not the slope along $AG$.
This is the angle at $G$, between $AG$ and the vertical. Subtract from $90°$ to get 14.8°.

parts.stem:
A roof is a pyramid on a square base of side 18 m, with its apex $V$ 12 m vertically above the centre $M$ of the base.
Calculate the angle between the slant edge $VA$ and the base.
hints: The slant edge ends at a corner, so the run along the base is half a diagonal.
$\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{12}{\sqrt{162}}\right) = 43.3\ldots$
parts.workedSolution: $AC = \sqrt{18^2 + 18^2} = \sqrt{648}$, so $AM^2 = 162$ and $AM = 12.7$ m. Then $\tan \angle VAM = \dfrac{12}{\sqrt{162}}$, so $\angle VAM = 43.3°$ (1 d.p.).

commonErrors.feedback: Half a base edge (9 m) was used, which answers part (b) instead: 53.1°. A slant edge runs to a corner, so use half the diagonal.
The whole diagonal was used. $M$ is the centre, so the run from $A$ is half of $AC$.

parts.stem: $N$ is the midpoint of $AB$. Calculate the angle between the sloping face $VAB$ and the base, and compare it with your answer to part (a).

scheme.for: $53.1°$, with a comparison: the face is steeper than the slant edge
scheme.examinerNote: Follow through the comparison from part (a).

hints: The face meets the base along $AB$, and the steepest line in it runs from $V$ to $N$.
$MN$ is half a base edge, 9 m.
Compare $\tan^{-1}\left(\tfrac{12}{9}\right)$ with your answer to (a): the smaller run gives the larger angle.
parts.workedSolution: $MN = 9$ m, so $\tan \angle VNM = \dfrac{12}{9}$ and $\angle VNM = 53.1°$. That is larger than the $43.3°$ in part (a): the same height stands over a shorter run, so the face is steeper than the slant edge.

commonErrors.feedback: Part (a) has been repeated. For a face the run is half an edge, 9 m, not half the diagonal, so the answer is 53.1°.
The whole base edge, 18 m, was used as the run. In triangle $NMV$ the run is from the centre $M$ out to $N$, which is half of that.

findTheMistake.stem: Caoimhe was asked how long the space diagonal $AG$ is in a cuboid measuring 7 cm by 4 cm by 6 cm. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Only two of the three dimensions went into the first line, so what has been found is $AC$, the diagonal of the base, not $AG$. The height of 6 cm never appears anywhere in the working. The first line should be $AG^2 = 7^2 + 4^2 + 6^2$, or the same thing in two steps: find $AC^2 = 65$ first, then $AG^2 = AC^2 + 6^2$.
findTheMistake.feedback: The method is sound and it has been aimed one dimension short, which is why the first mark still stands: 65 is exactly the intermediate value a two-step solution needs. Before you press the root key, count the dimensions in your line and check there are three. Summer 2025 examiners reported that most candidates could find the diagonal, so this is a habit worth locking in rather than a hard idea.

findTheMistake.stem: Jack was asked for the angle that $AG$ makes with the base $ABCD$ in a cuboid with $AB = 10$ cm, $BC = 5$ cm and $CG = 4$ cm. His working:
studentWorking: Angle between AG and the base = angle GAB
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The diagonal is right and the angle is not. $\angle GAB$ is measured from the edge $AB$, but the shadow of $AG$ on the base is the base diagonal $AC$, not an edge. The angle asked for is $\angle GAC$, and the triangle that contains it is $ACG$, right-angled at $C$.
correction: Angle between AG and the base = angle GAC
findTheMistake.feedback: The first line earns its mark, and the answer is then 21.8° instead of 19.7°. Examiners in both Summer 2023 and Summer 2025 reported this as the step that separates the grades: about half the candidates could point to the correct angle. Shine a torch straight down on $AG$ and ask what line the shadow falls on; that line is the one the angle is measured from.

findTheMistake.stem: Orla was asked for the angle between a sloping face and the base of a pyramid with a square base of side 16 cm and a vertical height of 15 cm. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Half the diagonal runs from the centre of the base out to a corner, so this is the angle the slant edge makes with the base. A face is measured along its line of greatest slope, from the apex down to the midpoint of a bottom edge, and the shadow of that line is half a base edge: 8 cm.
correction: N is the midpoint of AB, so MN = 8 cm
findTheMistake.feedback: Both angles are real angles of this pyramid: 53.0° for the slant edge and 61.9° for the face, and the face is always the steeper. A quick sketch of the base square with the centre, a corner and the midpoint of a side marked on it settles which run you need before any trigonometry starts.

prompts.prompt: The three moves in every 3-D question.
prompts.answer: 1 Find the right-angled triangle that contains what you want. 2 Draw it again on its own, with its three vertices and the lengths you know. 3 Use Pythagoras for a length, or a trigonometric ratio for an angle, keeping every value exact until the answer line.

prompts.prompt: The space diagonal of a cuboid with dimensions $a$, $b$ and $c$.
prompts.answer: $d = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}$, because $d^2 = (a^2 + b^2) + c^2$: the base diagonal first, then the height.

prompts.prompt: What does the angle between a line and a plane mean?
prompts.answer: The angle between the line and its shadow on the plane, where the shadow is what you would see if light came straight down onto the plane. For a space diagonal on the base of a cuboid the shadow is the base diagonal.

prompts.prompt: A cuboid $ABCDEFGH$ has $E$ above $A$ and $G$ above $C$. Which angle is the angle between $AG$ and the base, and which two are the tempting ones?
prompts.answer: $\angle GAC$. The tempting ones are $\angle GAB$, measured from an edge instead of from the diagonal, and $\angle AGC$, which is $90°$ minus the angle you want.

prompts.prompt: In a square-based pyramid, which base length goes with the slant edge, and which goes with a sloping face?
prompts.answer: Slant edge: half the base diagonal, because the edge ends at a corner. Sloping face: half the base edge, because the line of greatest slope ends at the midpoint of a side. The face angle is always the steeper of the two.
keyWords: half the diagonal for the edge
half the edge for the face

prompts.prompt: How do you set out a 3-D solution so a marker can follow it?
prompts.answer: Mark the triangle on the given diagram, then redraw it beside your working with its letters and known lengths, name the angle in three letters, write the ratio with numbers, and put one rounded answer on the answer line.

prompts.prompt: You have found a diagonal of $\sqrt{97}$ and need an angle. What do you type?
prompts.answer: $\sqrt{97}$ itself, not 9.8 and not 10. Rounding before the last step moves the angle by a tenth of a degree or more and loses the accuracy mark.

prompts.prompt: A cube has edge $x$. Write its space diagonal, and then the edge of a cube whose space diagonal is 9 cm.
prompts.answer: Space diagonal $= x\sqrt{3}$, since $x^2 + x^2 + x^2 = 3x^2$. If $x\sqrt{3} = 9$ then $3x^2 = 81$, $x^2 = 27$ and $x = 3\sqrt{3}$ cm.

prompts.prompt: How are the radius, the vertical height and the slant height of a cone related?
prompts.answer: $l^2 = r^2 + h^2$: they form a right-angled triangle with the slant height as the hypotenuse, so the slant height is always longer than the vertical height.
keyWords: l squared equals r squared plus h squared

prompts.prompt: You know all three sides of the extracted triangle. Which ratio should you choose for the angle?
prompts.answer: The one whose two sides you were given or found exactly, which is usually tangent with the height over the base diagonal. Choosing a ratio that uses a value you rounded earlier is how accuracy marks are lost.
keyWords: tangent with height over base diagonal

findings.asked: Length of a space diagonal, then the angle it makes with the base.
findings.wentWrong: Two thirds got the diagonal; only half could point to the correct angle, though most of those then used the right ratio.
findings.rule: The angle with the base lies between the space diagonal and the base diagonal.

findings.asked: Angle between a space diagonal and the base.
findings.wentWrong: Over half got full marks and nearly all started sensibly.
findings.rule: Two Pythagoras steps, then one trig ratio in the vertical right-angled triangle.

findings.asked: Space diagonal, then the angle with the base.
findings.wentWrong: Most found the diagonal; under half identified the required angle.
findings.rule: Sketch the right-angled triangle containing the angle separately.

findings.wentWrong: About 40% full marks for well-laid-out solutions; most earned some credit.
findings.rule: Label each 2D triangle you extract from the solid.

insight.ruleToRemember: Find the base diagonal with Pythagoras, then the space diagonal; the angle with the base sits in the vertical triangle made by the height, the base diagonal and the space diagonal - draw that triangle on its own.
insight.aStarSignal: Identifying the correct angle without a prompt and extracting the 2D triangle cleanly.
